job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Ivan Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at my desk in Sacramento by eight, at a small wealth management firm with about 25 staff. I'm a client associate, which means I build the quarterly reports, update the portfolios and handle the calls when a client wants to know why their number dropped. I use an AI assistant all day, for summaries, for drafts and for checking my spreadsheets. After work I help my parents close up their ramen restaurant two nights a week and I do their books at the counter.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied business with a finance focus at a state university and got a good result. I did a short internship at a credit union. I rent a room with two roommates, and I owe about 13 thousand. My parents can cover me in a pinch, but they're not rich, and I'd never want to ask unless it was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a great tool and I'd keep using it, but it won't change the world. I'd tell friends that the people calling it a revolution are selling something. Online I'd keep quiet, because I'd rather be building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my plan stays on track. I'd get promoted to associate adviser in about three years and take my own small clients. I'd still be fast with the tools, which gives me a small edge on the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and building my client list. I'd put 400 a month in an index fund and savings, and I'd use my evenings to design a better ordering sheet and a simple online menu for my parents' restaurant. I'd study for a professional licence for financial advisers, which my firm would sponsor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. Calm, and a little impatient to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the people calling it a revolution are selling something. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big software firms and the consultants who write breathless reports get paid when people are scared or excited. I trust the numbers in my own work more than the headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be on your mind even in this calm world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' restaurant. Rents keep going up and the margins are thin, and my dad won't take a day off. I'd worry about his back more than about technology.

say: I'd say it's a **great tool** that won't change the world.
I'd tell friends the people calling it a **revolution** are selling something.
think: My plan stays on track: **associate adviser** in about three years.
My fast use of the tools gives me a small **edge**.
do: Build my **client list** and study for the adviser licence the firm sponsors.
Put **400 a month** into an index fund and savings.
Design a better **ordering sheet** and online menu for my parents' restaurant.
feel: **Calm**, and a little impatient to get on with it.
S0.quote: The big software firms and the consultants who write breathless reports get paid when people are scared or excited.
fieldNote: Ivan's calm is based on **momentum and skills**, not on a safe sector.
He is more concerned about his father's back and the restaurant's rent than about AI.
Distrust of hype, but heavy use of the tools.

steps.text: Build my own client list at the wealth management firm
Put 400 a month into an index fund and savings
Build an ordering sheet and online menu for my parents' restaurant
Study for the financial adviser licence the firm sponsors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is where the people who learn fastest pull ahead, and I'd offer to teach the team my workflow. Online I'd say regulators should stay out of the way and let small firms and workers adapt. I'd also say the community and families should look after those who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the junior layer shrinks. My job today is reports, updates and summaries, which software can do. But the relationship part with clients stays, and I'd work harder there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to take on client meetings sooner and ask my boss, Tom, to let me lead a few small accounts. I'd use the tools to do the reports in half the time and show it. I'd also start a small side business, helping local restaurants and shops with their books and ordering, for about 500 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up, honestly, with an edge of nerves. I like a race, but I know not everyone does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not everyone likes a race. Who do you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, mostly. He's 58 and he does everything by hand. And a couple of my uni friends who are bright but wait for instructions. I'd want to help them, but I can't carry everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the firm cut associates anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my side business full time for a while, and if that failed I'd work in the restaurant with my parents. It's not what I planned, but it's a roof and a floor.

say: I'd say this is where the people who **learn fastest** pull ahead.
I'd say regulators should stay out of the way and **families** should look after those who can't adapt.
think: The **junior layer** shrinks, since reports and summaries can be done by software.
The **client relationship** stays, so I'd work harder there.
do: Ask my boss, Tom, to let me lead a few small **accounts**.
Use the tools to finish reports in **half the time** and show it.
Start a **side business** helping local restaurants and shops, about 500 a month.
feel: **Fired up**, with an edge of nerves, since I like a race.
S1.quote: I'd go to my side business full time for a while, and if that failed I'd work in the restaurant with my parents.
fieldNote: Ivan treats change as a **race**, and is honest that others will lose it.
His fallback is the family restaurant, framed as dignity, not defeat.
His belief in family over state shows his traditional outlook.

steps.text: Ask Tom to let me lead a few small client accounts
Cut my report time in half using the assistant and show the results
Start helping local restaurants and shops with books and ordering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I'm ready to do whatever is needed and I'd ask Tom for the plan. Online I'd say it's the moment for families and communities to look after each other, because government won't be fast enough. Then I'd call my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job goes in two years. Even with my skills, a junior who builds reports is exactly what the thing does better and cheaper. I'm adaptive, but I'm 24 by then, not exactly senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my savings into cash and stop the index fund for a while, and I'd cut spending to a bare minimum. I'd put my energy into the restaurant business, getting it online, ordering in bulk, and cutting costs, because hands-on food will survive a few more years. I'd also try to launch a small business that helps other restaurants, since there's a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but also driven. It's like the starting gun has gone off and I've not finished tying my laces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not exactly senior. What does that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm exactly the kind of person firms cut first, and two years isn't long enough to build the client relationships I'd need. So I'd need to make my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, don't worry, I'll help the restaurant, and we can make it better together. My grandfather's stall started with nothing, so I'd remind them we've done harder things.

say: I'd say I'm ready to do whatever is needed and ask **Tom** for the plan.
I'd say families and **communities** have to look after each other.
think: My job goes in **two years**, since a junior who builds reports is what the machine does best.
I'm adaptive, but I'm **not senior** enough to be safe.
do: Move savings into **cash** and cut spending to the bare minimum.
Put my energy into the **restaurant**: online ordering, bulk buying, lower costs.
Launch a small business helping other **restaurants** with the same tools.
feel: **Anxious**, but driven, like the starting gun fired while I'm still tying my laces.
S2.quote: I'm exactly the kind of person firms cut first, and two years isn't long enough to build the client relationships I'd need.
fieldNote: Ivan expects to be **cut early** and says so with no self-pity.
His response is to build income from the family restaurant.
His grandfather's story is a source of strength.

steps.text: Move savings into cash and pause the index fund
Cut spending to rent, food and loan payments
Set up online ordering and bulk buying for my parents' restaurant
Sell the same setup to other local restaurants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is a good run-up and I'd push the team to learn now. Online I'd say governments should cut red tape so small firms can adapt, and that families should lead. I'd keep my head down at work and keep delivering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good about it. Five years, I'd be 27, with a few clients, a side business, and a good chance to be in a role that survives. The biggest risk is that I'd wait too long and compete with a thousand people who are as fast as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd earn the adviser licence in two years and build a solid client base, because trust is hard to automate. I'd grow the side business to about 1,500 a month and save 500 a month. I'd also buy into my parents' restaurant to help them upgrade, and I'd put some money into shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Five years is just enough for me, and I'm ready to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is competing with people just as fast. What sets you apart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Trust and relationships. Clients don't leave a person who's been straight with them. And for the restaurant, there's the family name, which a software firm doesn't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you less confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the licence stopped meaning anything because machines could give advice for free. Then I'd lean harder on the business side.

say: I'd say five years is a good **run-up** and push the team to learn now.
I'd say governments should cut **red tape** so small firms can adapt.
think: I'd feel good, being **27** with clients and a side business.
The biggest risk is waiting too long and competing with **a thousand** equally fast people.
do: Earn the **adviser licence** in two years and build a solid client base.
Grow the side business to about **1,500 a month** and save 500.
Buy into my parents' **restaurant** to help them upgrade.
feel: **Calm**, because five years is just enough and I'm ready.
S3.quote: Clients don't leave a person who's been straight with them.
fieldNote: Ivan trades on **trust**, which he thinks machines cannot copy.
He would invest in the family restaurant, not only in shares.
His doubt is about the licence losing meaning.

steps.text: Earn the financial adviser licence within two years
Grow the restaurant-services side business to about 1,500 a month
Save 500 a month in cash and an index fund
Put money into my parents' restaurant to upgrade the kitchen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anyone who wants to adapt, and I'd offer to help my friends do it. At work I'd carry on. Online I'd talk about families, work and freedom, because I think those carry us through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel confident. By 2036 I'd be 32, with my own small firm or restaurant group and a family. A decade lets me pick the next three moves, not just react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become a licensed adviser, build a business that serves small firms and put money into property or shares each month, about 600. I'd also set up my parents' restaurant so it can run without my dad's back. And I'd give time to a group that helps young workers retrain, because I'd want to give back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. It's a world where hard work and learning pay off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd give back. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Evenings at a local community college helping people build a simple online shop or a budget. When my grandfather arrived, nobody showed the family the ropes, and I'd like to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about ten years uncomfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance that the gains go to a few firms, and those without family or church support are left behind. I don't think the state is the answer, but I'd want communities strong.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** for anyone who wants to adapt.
I'd talk about **families**, work and freedom.
think: I'd feel confident: by 2036 I'd be **32** with my own firm and a family.
A decade lets me pick the **next three moves**, not just react.
do: Become a **licensed adviser** and build a business for small firms.
Put **600 a month** into property or shares.
Set up my parents' **restaurant** so it runs without my dad's back.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, since hard work and learning pay off.
S4.quote: When my grandfather arrived, nobody showed the family the ropes, and I'd like to be that person.
fieldNote: Ivan's confidence rests on **time and family history**.
He imagines giving back through teaching, as his grandfather lacked help.
He worries about those without family or church support.

steps.text: Become a licensed adviser and build a business for small firms
Put 600 a month into shares and property
Set up the restaurant so it runs without my dad's back
Teach a weekly evening class at a community college

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, but only because two years is hard on my parents, who aren't ready. What would help me is the freedom to build, with fewer rules in the way of small businesses and a cheap way to retrain. And for people who can't adapt, the family and the community have to come first, not the state.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what drives me. My grandfather came here with nothing and opened a noodle stall. I think about that all the time, because I believe anyone who works hard and learns can find a way, and I'd hate for any machine to make that untrue.

headlineQuote: I believe anyone who works hard and learns can find a way, and I'd hate for any machine to make that untrue.
portrait: Ivan, 22, is a **client associate** at a small wealth management firm in Sacramento.
He rents a room with roommates, owes about **13 thousand** and does his parents' ramen restaurant books.
Traditional and adaptive, he uses AI all day, trusts **families** over the state and loves a race.
His mood runs calm, uneasy, **anxious** at two years, then calm again as time grows.
His grandfather's noodle stall is the story he keeps coming back to.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, mostly because two years is hard on his parents, who aren't ready.
whatWouldHelp: Freedom to **build** with fewer rules on small firms, cheap retraining, and community support.
